elements.content: Can you tell a real message from a fake one? Learn three habits that stop most scams, then test yourself.
Harborview Logistics is a made-up company. Every message in this course is fictional.

cues.text: You're Sam.
You work in accounts at Harborview Logistics, and it's Monday morning, just before nine.
You open your inbox.
Over the next few minutes you'll decide what's real, what's fake, and what to do if one gets past you.

elements.content: You are Sam, an accounts clerk at Harborview Logistics. It is Monday, 8:52. Coffee in hand, you open your inbox.
A message that pretends to be someone you trust, to trick you into clicking or paying, is called phishing. Today you will meet some.
Your job: decide what is real, what is fake, and what to do when something slips through.

cues.text: It's Tuesday, ten fourteen.
A text arrives from a number you don't know.
It says it's Dana, the CEO, and it asks you for gift cards.
What do you do?

elements.content: SCENARIO 1  ·  A TEXT FROM THE CEO
Sam, it is Dana. I am in a meeting and cannot talk. I need 5 gift cards, $100 each, for a client today. Buy them and text me the codes. I will pay you back. Do not call.

elements.label: Buy the cards. It is the CEO.
Call Dana on the number in the staff directory
Ignore it and delete the text

cues.text: You bought the cards.
Within minutes the codes were spent, and that money can't be recovered.
A real executive doesn't ask for gift cards by text.
And if someone asks you to keep it quiet, treat that as a warning in itself.

elements.content: You spent $500 and texted the codes. Within minutes they were used, and nobody can get the money back. Real executives do not ask for gift cards by text, and a request to keep it quiet is a warning sign of its own.
Takeaway: No real executive asks for gift cards by text. Check before you pay.

cues.text: You replied.
That told the sender your number works, and that you're willing to talk, so the messages got pushier.
If you don't trust a message, don't reply to it.
Check another way.

elements.content: Now they know you will answer
Replying told the sender your number works and that you are willing to talk. The messages got more insistent. Do not reply to a message you do not trust. Check it another way.
Takeaway: Do not reply to a message you do not trust. Check another way.

cues.text: You called Dana on the number from the staff directory.
She picked up, and she hadn't sent anything.
You also reported the text, and IT warned the team before lunch.
That's exactly the right move.

elements.content: Dana picked up. She had sent nothing. You chose the number yourself, so the criminal was never in the conversation. You also reported the text to IT, who warned the rest of the team before lunch.
Takeaway: Check with the person on a channel you already trust, then report it.

cues.text: You ignored it.
That kept you safe, which is good.
But the same text went to your whole team, and nobody warned them.
Deleting protects you.
Reporting protects everyone.

elements.content: Safe for you, not for everyone
You did not lose anything, which is good. But the same text went to your whole team, and nobody was warned. Deleting stops the harm to you. Reporting stops it for everyone.
Takeaway: Deleting protects you. Reporting protects everyone.

cues.text: Wednesday morning, just after nine.
Last night you opened a delivery notice, clicked the link, and typed in your work password.
It looked right at the time.
Now you're not so sure.
What do you do?

elements.content: SCENARIO 2  ·  I THINK I CLICKED SOMETHING
Last night you opened a "delivery notice", clicked the link and typed your work password into a page that looked right. This morning you feel uneasy about it.
It happens to careful people. What matters now is the next ten minutes.

elements.label: Do nothing and hope it is fine
Change your password and tell IT right now
Delete the email and forget about it

cues.text: You waited.
At two in the morning, someone signed in with your password and set up a rule to forward your email.
Nobody could shut it down, because nobody knew.
Every hour made it worse.

elements.content: At 2 a.m. someone signed in with your password, read your email and set a rule to forward your messages. Because you did not tell IT, nobody could shut it down. Every hour makes it worse.
Takeaway: Tell IT the moment you think you clicked. Every hour counts.

cues.text: You changed your password, then told IT straight away.
They saw one sign-in from a country you've never been to, signed it out, and checked your account.
Nothing was taken.
Turning on multi-factor authentication would have stopped it even sooner.

elements.content: You changed your password, then told IT. They saw one sign-in from a country you have never been to, signed it out, and checked your account. Nothing was taken. Turning on multi-factor authentication would have stopped it even earlier.
Takeaway: Change your password, tell IT, and turn on multi-factor authentication.

cues.text: You deleted the email.
That didn't change the fact that the criminal has your password, and they used it later that day.
Deleting hides the evidence from you, not from them.

elements.content: The email is gone, the password is not
Deleting the message did not change the fact that the criminal has your password. They used it later that day. Deleting hides the evidence from you, not from them.
Takeaway: Deleting an email does not take back what you typed into it.

cues.text: You made the safe call most of the time.
Now the goal is to make it a habit, so it still works on a busy Monday.

elements.content: You made the safe call more often than not. The next step is turning those instincts into habits you do without thinking, so they work even on a busy Monday.

cues.text: A few of your choices put you or your team at risk.
That's why we practice here, where a wrong turn costs nothing.
The three habits coming up would have changed those moments.

elements.content: A few choices put you, or your team, at risk. That is exactly why we practice here, where a wrong turn costs nothing. The three habits next would have changed those moments.

cues.text: Three habits.
Pause.
Take ten seconds before you click, open, or pay, and ask yourself why the rush.
Check.
Read the sender's address letter by letter, hover over links, and if it matters, confirm another way, using a number or a channel you already have.
Report.
Send it to IT, even if you didn't fall for it.
One report protects everyone.

elements.content: Three habits that stop most scams
Urgency is the hook. Take ten seconds before you click, open or pay, and ask: why the rush?
Read the sender address letter by letter and hover over links. If it matters, confirm another way, using a number or channel you already have.
Use the report button or forward it to IT, even if you did not fall for it. One report protects everyone.
Select the card to turn it over.

terms.definition: A message that pretends to be from someone you trust, to trick you into clicking a link, opening a file, giving up a password or paying money.
Phishing by text message. The word joins SMS and phishing.
Phishing by phone call. The caller pretends to be your bank, your boss or a support team.
Phishing aimed at one person or one team, using details about them to look real.
The part of an address after the @ in an email, or after the // in a web page. Criminals register domains that look almost the same as a real one.
Signing in with your password plus a second proof, such as a code on your phone. It can stop a thief who has only your password.
